claims.claim: You can learn as much about God from the natural world as from books.
Kindness to animals is part of a holy life.

stances.summary: I have no need of other books. The created world is my book, it is always open, and in it I read the words of God whenever I want.
stances.quote: 'My book, O philosopher,' replied Anthony, 'is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.'
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF second series vol. 2, 1890 (Socrates Scholasticus, Church History)
stances.original: Τὸ ἐμὸν βιβλίον, ἕφη ὁ Ἀντώνιος, ὦ φιλόσοφε, ἡ φύσις τῶν γεγονότων ἐστι: καὶ πάρεστιν, ὅτε βούλομαι, τοὺς λόγους ἀναγινώσκειν τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ. (Socrates, as transcribed by the First1KGreek project, with its own typos: ἕφη for ἔφη)
stances.work: Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos, chapter 92, as quoted by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History
stances.context: A philosopher asked Antony how he could bear to live without the comfort of books. Evagrius recorded the answer in the Praktikos (c. 390) among sayings of the desert fathers; Socrates copied it c. 440. Evagrius came to Egypt c. 383 and never met Antony (d. 356), so this is a saying handed down in the desert, not an eyewitness record. It is not in Athanasius' Life of Antony, but it fits it: Antony had little or no schooling in letters (Life 1, 72-73), and told philosophers who mocked him for it: 'Whoever, therefore, has a sound mind has not need of letters' (Life 73). He was not against Scripture: he memorised it by hearing ('his memory served him for books', Life 3) and told his monks 'The Scriptures are enough for instruction' (Life 16). So his point is that creation is a book anyone can read, not that Scripture is unnecessary.

stances.summary: Nature was the first book God gave to rational beings. Written teaching was only added after we went astray.
stances.quote: The first book given by God to the rational beings, is the nature of the created things. Written teachings have been added only after aberration.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, Royal Academy, 1923)
stances.work: Ascetical Homilies (Mystic Treatises), "Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence"
stances.location: Discourse V, Wensinck p. 61 (his index: "Nature is the first book given to man 61")
stances.context: Isaac of Nineveh (late 7th century) was a bishop and hermit of the Church of the East, which Chalcedonian and Miaphysite churches called Nestorian; he is now read and honoured across Orthodoxy. The same discourse opens: 'God has made great the honour of man, by the twofold teachings he has given him', and says: 'Ask from nature a true witness concerning thyself, then thou wilt not err. If thou goest yet astray, let thyself be taught by that second witness'. So Scripture is the second, corrective witness, given because we strayed. Isaac still urges the reading of Scripture on solitaries elsewhere. The djvu text is an OCR of the 1923 print, with line breaks inside the sentence; the words match once whitespace is normalised. Wensinck died in 1939; the translation is public domain in the US (published before 1929) and in the EU.

stances.summary: God first taught people through things, not letters. The sky is a book that the poor, the unlettered and foreigners can all read, and it teaches enough.
stances.quote: Upon this volume the unlearned, as well as the wise man, shall be alike able to look; the poor man as well as the rich man; and wherever any one may chance to come, there looking upwards towards the heavens, he will receive a sufficient lesson from the view of them
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF first series vol. 9, 1889
stances.location: Homily 9, section 5 (see also section 3 and Homily 10, section 3)
stances.context: Preached at Antioch in Lent 387. Asked why the Scriptures came so late (with Moses, not Adam), he answers in section 3: 'It was because God was desirous of instructing the nature of man, not by letters, but by things. But what does the expression by things signify? By means of the Creation itself.' Section 5 adds that a book would have helped only the literate, the rich who can buy a Bible, and speakers of its language, while the Scythian, the Barbarian, the Indian and the Egyptian can all read the sky. He is not against Scripture: in the same homily he says the Scriptures are 'most useful and most necessary'. Homily 10.3 repeats that God 'instructed our race, stretching out the heavens, and there openly unfolding a vast volume'.

stances.summary: Some people read a book to find God. But creation itself is a great book. God did not write in ink; He put what He made in front of your eyes, and heaven and earth cry out that He made them.
stances.quote: Another person reads a book to find God. But there is a great book: the very appearance of created things. Look above and below, pay attention, read. God did not make letters of ink for you to know Him by. He set before your eyes the very things He made. Why look for a louder voice? Heaven and earth cry out to you: God made me.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (the only English, Edmund Hill in The Works of Saint Augustine, is copyrighted)
stances.original: Alius, ut inveniat Deum, librum legit. Est quidam magnus liber ipsa species creaturae: superiorem et inferiorem contuere, attende, lege. Non Deus, unde eum cognosceres, de atramento litteras fecit: ante oculos tuos posuit haec ipsa quae fecit. Quid quaeris maiorem vocem? Clamat ad te caelum et terra: Deus me fecit.
stances.context: The sermon goes on: 'You read what Moses wrote. What did Moses himself read so that he could write? Look piously at heaven and earth' (own rendering). He then warns, from Romans 1, that pagan philosophers did reach the Creator through creation but were blamed because they did not glorify Him or give thanks. The same image appears in Against Faustus 32.20, public-domain English: 'had you begun with looking on the book of nature as the production of the Creator of all' (Stothert, NPNF 1st series vol. 4, 1887; Latin 'quasi legens magnum quemdam librum naturae rerum'). Compare Confessions 10.6: 'My questioning was my observing of them; and their beauty was their reply' (Pilkington, NPNF). CAUTION: his other famous 'book of the world' lines, Expositions on the Psalms 45.7 ('Liber tibi sit pagina divina... liber tibi sit orbis terrarum') and Letter 43.25 ('We have a greater book, the world itself'), are about the worldwide Church as fulfilled prophecy, not about nature. Do not use them for this claim. augustinus.it blocks plain curl; fetch it with a browser User-Agent.

stances.summary: The world was made as a school for souls, where they learn to know God, because the sight of visible things leads the mind by the hand to invisible ones.
stances.quote: since it is really the school where reasonable souls exercise themselves, the training ground where they learn to know God; since by the sight of visible and sensible things the mind is led, as by a hand, to the contemplation of invisible things.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF second series vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Hexaemeron (Homilies on the Six Days of Creation)
stances.context: Lenten homilies preached at Caesarea c. 378. Basil reads creation with Moses as his guide, and warns (Homily 1.4) that astronomers who measured the stars 'have discovered all except one thing: the fact that God is the Creator of the universe'. So nature studied without God misses Him. Letter 235.1 states the order of knowing: 'in our belief about God, first comes the idea that God is. This we gather from His works' (NPNF). Homily 9 draws moral lessons from animals ('Does not the gratitude of the dog shame all who are ungrateful to their benefactors?'). Marked strength 1 because he never ranks nature above or equal to Scripture.

stances.summary: Even without other teaching, creation by its order and harmony announces its Maker as plainly as writing does.
stances.quote: yet it is further possible to attain to the knowledge of God from the things which are seen, since Creation, as though in written characters, declares in a loud voice, by its order and harmony, its own Lord and Creator.
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF second series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written c. 335. The sentence begins 'Or, if the soul's own teaching is insufficient': the first path is the soul looking into itself, creation is the second. In the companion work On the Incarnation 12, creation was given to remind careless man of God, and then 'a law, and prophets' were sent for those not ready to look up to heaven, 'For men are able to learn from men more directly about higher things'. So he thinks creation is enough for anyone who looks, and books are a further mercy for the weak. Chapter 35 uses the sculptor Phidias: the artist is known by his works even when absent.

stances.summary: God cannot be seen with the eyes, but He is perceived through His providence and works, as a pilot is inferred from a ship steering into harbour.
stances.quote: so God cannot indeed be seen by human eyes, but is beheld and perceived through His providence and works.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Apology to a pagan friend, c. 180, by the bishop of Antioch. Not in the candidate pool. Book 1 chapter 6 is titled "God is Known by His Works". Like most apologists he then turns to the prophets for fuller knowledge.

stances.summary: We see God not only in His hidden being but through the greatness of His creation, His justice and His daily providence.
stances.quote: For we not only discover God by admiring His incomprehensible essence, a thing which still lies hid in the hope of the promise, but we see Him through the greatness of His creation, and the consideration of His justice, and the aid of His daily providence
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF second series vol. 11, 1894
stances.location: Conference 1 (First Conference of Abbot Moses), chapter 15
stances.context: Spoken in the Conference by Abba Moses of Scetis, as Cassian reconstructed it c. 425 from visits c. 385-399. Whether this Moses is Moses the Black is disputed; do not credit it to Moses the Black. Creation is one of many ways of contemplating God in the list, alongside His dealings with the saints, His mercy, grace and the Incarnation. It is not a claim that nature teaches as much as Scripture.

stances.summary: The order of the world could not hold together unless One joined and kept it. That power I call God.
stances.quote: This world could never have taken shape as a single system out of parts so diverse and opposite were it not that there is One who joins together these so diverse things.
stances.translation: H. R. James, 1897 (Project Gutenberg)
stances.context: Written in prison c. 524 by a Christian (author of theological tractates on the Trinity). Here the speaker is Boethius himself answering Lady Philosophy. The whole Consolation reasons its way to God from the order of the world and from reason, without once quoting Scripture, which is why it is a real witness to the view that God can be known from nature. It says nothing directly about books versus nature.

stances.summary: Creation itself makes the argument for God, speaking to the eye and the heart. But on anything beyond that, Scripture is the rule and measure of every belief.
stances.quote: The Creation proclaims outright the Creator; for the very heavens, as the Prophet says, declare the glory of God with their unutterable words.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection (a dialogue with his sister Macrina)
stances.location: Early in the dialogue, her answer to the Epicurean objection
stances.context: Macrina says this is 'an argument which is not mine nor that of any human being ... but an argument which the whole Creation enunciates by the medium of its wonders'. Later in the same dialogue she says: 'we make the Holy Scriptures the rule and the measure of every tenet'. So creation proves that God is; Scripture governs every doctrine beyond that. The dialogue was written by Gregory after her death (379/380); how closely it keeps her words is debated.

stances.summary: Our eyes and the law of nature teach us that God exists and holds all things together. What God is, no one has found out, and even Scripture gives only a little more light.
stances.quote: Now our very eyes and the Law of Nature teach us that God exists and that He is the Efficient and Maintaining Cause of all things
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF second series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Preached at Constantinople in 380. Section 16: reason 'leads us up to God through visible things'. Section 17: 'What God is in nature and essence, no man ever yet has discovered', and even one who 'has had the testimony of Scripture to his knowledge of God' has only a relative advantage over others. So nature and Scripture both fall short of God's essence; Scripture gives somewhat more.

stances.summary: Creation shows everyone that God made it, but the revelation of the Father through the Word gives far more life than creation does.
stances.quote: For if the manifestation of God which is made by means of the creation, affords life to all living in the earth, much more does that revelation of the Father which comes through the Word, give life to those who see God.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: The same sentence opens with the famous 'For the glory of God is a living man'. Elsewhere: 'For even creation reveals Him who formed it' (2.9.1); creation, the law and prophets, and the incarnate Word are successive revelations (4.6.6); and 'the Scriptures are indeed perfect' while even things 'which lie at our very feet' in nature transcend our knowledge (2.28.2). Graded view: creation first, the Word most fully.

stances.summary: Nature and Scripture are twin witnesses, and both are clear. But nature is hard for us and Scripture is easy, and it was not from nature that we learned Christ.
stances.quote: And though nature is hard to us in every thing, the Scripture is able to teach us of the Father and the Son
stances.translation: J. B. Morris, Select Works of S. Ephrem the Syrian (Library of the Fathers vol. 41), 1847
stances.work: Rhythms upon the Faith, against the Disputers (the Hymns on Faith)
stances.context: The same stanza says 'Nature is before thy hand, Scripture before thine eyes, and nature is hard for us, Scripture is easy for us; for it was not from nature that we learnt Christ' (the OCR there is broken by margin notes, so the clean sentence was chosen as the quote). The stanza that follows asks who can search out animals, trees and the olive, and says such search 'ends in stillness'. Yet in Rhythm 35 he opens 'Like is nature unto Scripture' and says 'Clear is nature, and clear is Scripture': outsiders stumbled over nature, insiders were perplexed by Scripture. His famous line about the two witnesses, Nature and Scripture, is Hymns on Paradise 5.2, available in English only in Sebastian Brock's copyrighted translation (1990), so it is not quoted here. The context is the 4th-century argument with those who 'searched' God's nature (Arians).

stances.summary: God is known first from nature, through His works. But He added a written revelation so that we could know Him, His plans and His will more fully and with more authority.
stances.quote: But, that we might attain an ampler and more authoritative knowledge at once of Himself, and of His counsels and will, God has added a written revelation for the benefit of every one whose heart is set on seeking Him, that seeking he may find, and finding believe, and believing obey.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: Sed quo plenius et impressius tam ipsum quam dispositiones eius et voluntates adiremus, adiecit instrumentum litteraturae, si qui velit de deo inquirere et inquisito invenire et invento credere et credito deservire.
stances.context: Written 197, before his Montanist years. Chapter 17 offers the proof of God 'from the works of His hands' and from 'the testimony of the soul', so nature is a real witness. Against Marcion 1.18 (c. 207, Montanist period) gives the order: 'We maintain that God must first be known from nature, and afterwards authenticated by instruction: from nature by His works; by instruction, through His revealed announcements' (Holmes, ANF 3; Latin 'Nos definimus deum primo natura cognoscendum, deinde doctrina recognoscendum'). Disagrees only with 'as much'.

stances.summary: The philosophers could not reach the truth about God by their own reasoning. The prophets alone saw it and wrote it down, and their writings still help anyone who believes them.
stances.quote: These alone both saw and announced the truth to men, neither reverencing nor fearing any man, not influenced by a desire for glory, but speaking those things alone which they saw and which they heard, being filled with the Holy Spirit. Their writings are still extant
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 155-160. Spoken by the old man by the sea in Justin's account of his own conversion from Platonism; Justin adopts it ('a flame was kindled in my soul', ch. 8). The argument (chs. 3-6) is that the soul cannot see God by its own natural power; knowledge comes through the prophets' writings. He is contrasting philosophy with Scripture more than nature with Scripture.

stances.summary: Anyone who looks at the sky can tell there is some providence, but not which God it is. Studying nature is guesswork. Only God's teaching gives wisdom.
stances.quote: That, therefore, which they perceived to be justly required by the demands of nature, but which they were themselves unable to perform, and saw that the philosophers could not effect, is accomplished only by divine instruction; for that only is wisdom.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.location: Book 3, chapter 26 (chapter title: "It is Divine Instruction Only Which Bestows Wisdom")
stances.context: Written c. 303-311. In 1.2 he grants that no one is so uncivilised that, raising his eyes to heaven, he does not see 'that there is some providence', 'although he knows not by the providence of what God all this visible universe is governed'. In 3.3 he calls those 'mad and senseless, who imagine that they know natural things, which cannot be known by man'. So nature shows that a providence exists; wisdom about God comes only from God's own teaching. Oddly, he adds that divine wisdom works with 'no need of payment, or books, or nightly studies', so he is not praising book-learning either.

stances.summary: My own reasoning about the world got me to one eternal God who cares for it. But the books of Moses and the prophets gave me an exact knowledge of God that reasoning could not reach.
stances.quote: I confess that I was amazed to find in them an indication concerning God so exact that it expressed in the terms best adapted to human understanding an unattainable insight into the mystery of the Divine nature.
stances.translation: E. W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF second series vol. 9, 1899
stances.context: Written c. 356-360. 'Them' are 'the books which, according to the tradition of the Hebrew faith, were written by Moses and the prophets'. Before finding them his mind, by reflection, had already rejected polytheism and concluded that God is one and does not neglect His world (1.4); after them he learned from Wisdom 13:5 to see God's beauty in created things (1.7), and he credits 'its own reflection and the teaching of Scripture' (1.8). The Gospel of John then takes him further (1.10-13). So reason and nature start the road; Scripture gives what they cannot.

stances.summary: Whoever does not know the Scriptures does not know Christ.
stances.quote: For if, as the apostle Paul says, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and whoever does not know the Scriptures does not know the power of God and His wisdom, then ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin (the only full English, T. P. Scheck 2015, is copyrighted)
stances.original: Si enim juxta apostolum Paulum (II Cor. I, 24) Christus Dei virtus est, Deique sapientia; et qui nescit Scripturas, nescit Dei virtutem ejusque sapientiam: ignoratio Scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est.
stances.context: Written c. 408-410, dedicated to Eustochium. Jerome does not discuss nature here; he is justifying a lifetime of Scripture study. Included because it is the strongest early statement that knowledge of Christ comes through the Scriptures, which the nature-as-book view does not supply. Use with care for this claim. (The Migne text cites 'II Cor.'; the verse is 1 Corinthians 1:24.)

stances.summary: A merciful heart burns for the whole creation, people, birds, beasts, even demons. It cannot bear to see any creature hurt, and it prays with tears even for reptiles.
stances.quote: And what is a merciful heart? He replied: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists;
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, Royal Academy, 1923)
stances.location: Treatise 74 in Wensinck, p. 341 (other editions number the homilies differently)
stances.context: Isaac gives this as the answer 'the same Father' gave when asked, and makes it his own; the treatise begins by defining purity as 'A heart full of mercy unto the whole created nature'. It continues: such a heart 'is not able to bear hearing or examining injury or any insignificant suffering of anything in the creation', and 'even in behalf of the irrational beings ... he offers prayers with tears that they may be guarded and strengthened; even in behalf of the kinds of reptiles'. Church of the East, late 7th century. Caution: his other famous animal passage (treatise 82, p. 386: the humble man approaches beasts of prey and they lick his hands, smelling Adam's scent before the fall) goes on to say he crushes deadly reptiles 'as if they were locusts'. That passage is about restored authority over beasts, not tenderness.

stances.summary: The saints are gentle to everyone, and their gentleness reaches even to animals. If they pity animals, how much more should we care for people.
stances.quote: For the souls of the Saints are very gentle and, loving unto man, both in regard to their own, and to strangers. And even to the unreasoning creatures they extend their gentleness.
stances.translation: J. Walker, J. Sheppard and H. Browne, revised by George B. Stevens, NPNF first series vol. 11, 1889
stances.location: Homily 29 (moral exhortation on pastors, after the example of Abraham)
stances.context: He goes on: 'Wherefore also a certain wise man said, The righteous pities the souls of his cattle. But if he does those of cattle, how much more those of men', and then shames lazy pastors with Cappadocian shepherds who lie buried under snow for their sheep. So gentleness to animals is a mark of the saint, used here to argue for care of souls. In Homily 21 on 1 Corinthians, on 'Does God care for oxen?', he says God 'does take care of them, but not so as to make a law concerning such a thing as this', and reads the ox law as 'training the Jews to mercy in the case of the brutes' and through them teaching care for teachers. The widely shared version that adds 'because they are of the same origin as ourselves' is not in this text (see misattributions).

stances.summary: God's Law is gentle even to animals: do not take a newborn from its mother, help up your enemy's fallen donkey. Such mildness trains people in gentleness and shames those who are cruel.
stances.quote: Let the Greeks, then, feel ashamed, and whoever else inveighs against the law; since it shows mildness in the case of the irrational creatures, while they expose the offspring of men
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 200. He praises the Mosaic laws on animals as 'training man to gentleness by what is beneath him, by means of the irrational creatures', and says whoever tears a newborn from its mother's milk 'dishonours nature'. The reason is largely for people's sake: 'much more in the case of men does it provide beforehand a cure for cruelty and savageness of disposition'. He also reads the ox-and-donkey yoke law as a lesson about not wronging people of another race.

stances.summary: When wild animals ruined his garden he did not harm them. He took hold of one gently and asked them, since he hurt none of them, not to hurt him.
stances.quote: But he, gently laying hold of one of them, said to them all, 'Why do you hurt me, when I hurt none of you? Depart, and in the name of the Lord come not near this spot.'
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF second series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Written by Athanasius c. 357-362, who knew Antony. The desert beasts, coming for water, were damaging the vegetables he grew for visitors; after his words they kept away. Chapter 51 applies Job 5:23: the wild beasts 'kept peace with him'. In Jerome's Life of Paul the Hermit 16, a literary and largely legendary work, Antony blesses the two lions that dug Paul's grave. The desert theme is mostly peace and authority over beasts, not animal welfare as such.

stances.summary: Seeing a worn-out hare about to be caught by hunting dogs, he pitied it and ordered the dogs to stop, and it escaped.
stances.quote: Now the blessed man pitied the danger of the creature with pious feelings, and commanded the dogs to give up following it, and to permit it to get safe away.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF second series vol. 11, 1894
stances.context: Written c. 404 by Sulpicius, who knew Martin; in the dialogue the story is told by Gallus, Martin's disciple, as an eyewitness ('we came upon a band of huntsmen'). The same chapter and the next draw moral lessons from animals (the shorn sheep, the diving birds as demons). Martin is shown commanding animals; the hare story is the one clear act of pity.

stances.summary: When he crushed a mosquito that bit him, he blamed himself for taking revenge and did six months of penance in a mosquito-filled marsh. He also healed a hyena's blind cub.
stances.quote: So, accusing himself for having taken vengeance, he condemned himself to sit naked for six months in the marsh of Scete, which is in the great desert.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Lausiac History of Palladius (SPCK), 1918
stances.context: Palladius (writing c. 420) lived near Macarius (d. c. 393) and knew him. Not in the candidate pool. The fault he punished was his own vengeful impulse, not the insect's death as such, so this is about purity of heart more than animal welfare. Section 27 (told by his disciple Paphnutius): a hyena brought her blind whelp; Macarius prayed and healed it, and she later brought him a fleece. The tertullian.org page states the text is public domain.

stances.summary: He told a monk to watch for an exhausted crane blown over from Ireland, to take it in and nurse it for three days, and blessed him for his kindness to it.
stances.quote: Treat that bird tenderly, take it to some neighbouring house, where it may be kindly received and carefully nursed and fed by thee for three days and three nights.
stances.translation: William Reeves, 1874 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
stances.location: Book 1, the crane chapter (1.48 in the standard numbering)
stances.context: Columba died 597; Adomnan, ninth abbot of Iona, wrote c. 697-700 from the monastery's memories. Not in the candidate pool. On the monk's return Columba says: 'God bless thee, my child, for thy kind attention to this foreign visitor'. His stated reason is partly that the bird 'cometh from our own native place'. In Book 3 (3.23), just before his death, his old white pack-horse lays its head on his breast and weeps; when his attendant tries to drive it off, he says: 'Let it alone, as it is so fond of me, let it pour out its bitter grief into my bosom.'

stances.person: Florentius of Nursia (hermit, via Gregory the Great)
stances.summary: A hermit whose tame bear herded his sheep called it his brother. When envious monks killed it, he grieved and cursed them, and later wept for having cursed.
stances.quote: very much grieved he was that the bear, whom in great simplicity he called his brother, came not home.
stances.translation: P.W. (1608), revised by Edmund G. Gardner, 1911
stances.context: Gregory wrote c. 593-594 from informants, about a 6th-century hermit. Not in the candidate pool. Florentius calls the killers men who 'killed my bear which did them no harm'; they die of leprosy. But Florentius grieved 'yet more the malice of the monks than the death of his bear', and Gregory's lesson is against cursing, so this tells us little about Gregory's own view of animals. In Dialogues 2.8 Gregory also reports that a crow came daily from the woods to take bread from Benedict's hand: a habit, not a stated teaching, and too thin to give Benedict a position.

stances.summary: We have no shared rights with animals. Refusing to kill them is superstition, and Christ Himself showed this when He sent the demons into the pigs.
stances.quote: your abstaining from the slaughter of animals and from injuring plants is shown by Christ to be mere superstition; for, on the ground that there is no community of rights between us and brutes and trees, He both sent the devils into an herd of swine, Matthew 8:32 and withered by His curse a tree
stances.translation: Richard Stothert, NPNF first series vol. 4, 1887
stances.work: On the Morals of the Manichaeans
stances.context: Written c. 388-390 against the Manichees, who forbade killing animals and plants because they held light-particles of the divine were trapped in them. He does not praise cruelty. In section 59 he grants: 'we see and hear by their cries that animals die with pain, although man disregards this in a beast, with which, as not having a rational soul, we have no community of rights.' He repeats the view much later in City of God 1.20 (c. 413): 'Thou shalt not kill' does not cover 'the irrational animals', which 'are therefore by the just appointment of the Creator subjected to us to kill or keep alive for our own uses'. (In the NPNF text the scripture reference 'Matthew 8:32' sits inside the quoted sentence; it is an editorial insertion.)

stances.summary: Animals are not dearer to God than people. The Creator made everything to serve rational beings: dogs to guard, oxen to plough, and even lions and bears to exercise our courage.
stances.quote: The Creator, then, has constituted all things the servants of the rational being and of his natural understanding.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written c. 248, answering the pagan Celsus, who argued that animals are wiser than humans and 'more beloved by God' (4.74-99). Origen mentions that 'We subdue by our gentle treatment those animals whose nature it is to be tamed', but as a means of use, and that we slaughter them when we need their flesh. He never calls kindness to animals a virtue. Origen was condemned after his death (Constantinople, 553) for other teachings (pre-existence of souls, universal restoration); mark as later judged heterodox.

splits_fathers: (a) Almost every Father held that creation shows that God exists and shows His power, wisdom and care (Romans 1:20 and Psalm 19 are the shared texts); nobody says nature teaches nothing. The real split is over 'as much'. A strong 'book of nature' voice exists: Antony (creation is my book), Isaac the Syrian (nature is the first book; Scripture was added after we strayed), Chrysostom (God taught by things, not letters; the sky is a book even the unlettered can read), and Augustine (God did not write in ink; creation is a great book). On the other side, many say nature shows THAT God is while Scripture, the prophets or Christ show WHO He is: Tertullian (written revelation is ampler and more authoritative), Justin, Lactantius, Hilary, Irenaeus, Ephrem ('it was not from nature that we learnt Christ') and Jerome ('ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ'). Many hold both at once (Basil, Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Macrina). Note that when the Fathers say 'books' they nearly always mean Scripture; only Antony and Chrysostom set nature against letters and literacy as such. (b) Where the Fathers speak of it, gentleness to animals is a mark of the saint: Chrysostom, Isaac, Clement, and the desert and Celtic lives (Antony, Macarius, Martin, Columba). Often the reason is human-centred (it trains mercy toward people: Clement, Chrysostom) or is really about a restored Adam whom the beasts obey (Isaac on the humble man, Antony, Gerasimus). The one clear opposing voice is Augustine, who says twice that there is 'no community of rights' between us and animals and calls refusing to kill them superstition; Origen says all creatures were made to serve rational beings. Nobody defends cruelty. So both claims have real voices on both sides, but in (b) the 'disagree' side rests mainly on Augustine.
splits_people_today: (a) Genuinely split. Many people, including many who never go to church and many who do, say they feel closest to God outdoors and learn about Him from nature; 'spiritual but not religious' people and nature-lovers would agree. Evangelical and traditional Christians usually rank Scripture above nature (nature shows God's power; only Scripture shows the gospel) and would disagree with 'as much'. Catholics hold that God can be known from creation by reason but that revelation is needed for more, so they would split. Some readers will take 'books' to mean book-learning in general rather than Scripture, which changes the answer. A good discriminating item. (b) Nearly one-sided today: almost everyone, Christian or not, thinks cruelty to animals is wrong and kindness is good, so most will agree. The real modern split is whether animals matter for their own sake and whether this is a matter of holiness rather than simple decency (animal-welfare Christians, vegetarians and people inspired by Francis of Assisi versus 'dominion', farming and hunting views that see animals as there for our use). The Fathers are more split on this than people today; as worded the statement will tell the quiz little, because the 'disagree' side today is small.

misattributions.line: O God, enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all living things, our brothers the animals, to whom Thou gavest the earth as their home in common with us...
misattributions.attributed_to: Basil the Great ("Prayer of St Basil for animals")
misattributions.truth: Written by Walter Rauschenbusch, 'For This World', in Prayers of the Social Awakening (Boston, 1910), p. 47: 'Enlarge within us the sense of fellowship with all the living things, our little brothers, to whom thou hast given this earth as their home in common with us.' Checked in the 1910 printing on archive.org (prayersofsociala00rausiala). No such prayer is in Basil's works.

misattributions.line: The Saints are exceedingly loving and gentle to mankind, and even to brute beasts... Surely we ought to show them great kindness and gentleness for many reasons, but, above all, because they are of the same origin as ourselves.
misattributions.attributed_to: John Chrysostom, Homily 29 on Romans (cited as NPNF vol. 11 p. 546, or as "Homily XXXIX:35")
misattributions.truth: Half real, half not. The NPNF text (checked in full on New Advent and in CCEL's complete text of NPNF1-11) says: 'the souls of the Saints are very gentle and, loving unto man ... And even to the unreasoning creatures they extend their gentleness', then quotes 'The righteous pities the souls of his cattle' and argues 'how much more those of men'. The sentence about showing animals kindness 'because they are of the same origin as ourselves' does not appear. Its source is unknown. Use only the NPNF wording.

misattributions.line: The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page.
misattributions.truth: Not found in Augustine. It appears in 'Select Proverbs of All Nations' (1824) and in John Feltham's paraphrase that Augustine said 'the world is a great book'. Augustine's real 'greater book' lines (Letter 43.25 and Expositions on the Psalms 45.7) are about the worldwide spread of the Church fulfilling prophecy, not travel and not nature (see fauxtations.wordpress.com, 'Augustine: The world is a book?').

misattributions.line: Let the divine page be a book for you... let the whole world be a book for you (Liber tibi sit pagina divina... liber tibi sit orbis terrarum), and 'We have a greater book, the world itself'
misattributions.attributed_to: Augustine, quoted as a "book of nature" text
misattributions.truth: Real words, wrong meaning. In Expositions on the Psalms 45.7 'haec' ('these things') are fulfilled prophecies about the Gospel reaching the nations, and in Letter 43.25 he reads in the world 'the accomplishment of that of which I read the promise in the Book of God' (Psalm 2:8). Both are anti-Donatist arguments from the Church's worldwide spread. Also, Confessions 13.15, often cited as nature-as-book ('the firmament of Your Book'), is an allegory in which the firmament is Scripture. For Augustine on the book of nature use Sermon 68.6 or Against Faustus 32.20. Note too that the NPNF English of Expositions on Psalm 46 (45) is abridged and omits the 'liber tibi sit' sentence.

misattributions.line: Isaac the Syrian on the merciful heart, cited as 'Mystic Treatises, Ch. 1, Homily 7' or 'Homily 7'
misattributions.attributed_to: Isaac the Syrian (a mis-citation, not a false attribution)
misattributions.truth: The passage is real but is treatise 74 in Wensinck's 1923 translation (p. 341); edition numberings differ, and it is not Homily 7. Isaac gives it as an elder's answer ('the same Father was asked') and adopts it. Popular excerpts of his companion passage on the humble man and wild beasts usually stop before he says the humble man crushes deadly reptiles 'as if they were locusts'.

misattributions.line: Columbanus in the forest choosing wild beasts over sinful men, cited as 'Vita St. Columbae, C.15'
misattributions.attributed_to: St Columba (Adomnan's Life of Columba), on the Pan-Orthodox Concern for Animals site
misattributions.truth: The wolves story is in Jonas of Bobbio's Life of Columbanus (chapter 15 in D. C. Munro's 1895 translation), about Columbanus (d. 615), not Columba of Iona (d. 597). It is also not about kindness to animals: the wolves tug at his clothes and leave.

notes: WORDING. In the Fathers 'books' almost always means Scripture. If the quiz says 'books', some players will hear 'book-learning', which only Antony (letters) and Chrysostom (literacy) address. The strongest reveal lines: for (a) agree, Antony's 'My book ... is the nature of things that are made', Isaac's 'The first book given by God ... is the nature of the created things', Chrysostom's 'not by letters, but by things', and Augustine's Sermon 68 ('God did not make letters of ink'); for (a) disagree, Ephrem's 'it was not from nature that we learnt Christ', Tertullian's 'ampler and more authoritative knowledge', and Jerome's 'ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ'. For (b) agree, Isaac's merciful heart; for (b) disagree, Augustine's 'no community of rights'. CHECKING. Two quotes are own renderings (Augustine Sermon 68, Jerome on Isaiah); check their 'original' field against the url, not the English. augustinus.it returns an error page to plain curl; use a browser User-Agent. The archive.org djvu texts (Isaac, Ephrem) are OCR with line breaks inside sentences: normalise whitespace before matching, and do not strip HTML tags from these .txt pages, because stray < and > characters in the OCR would delete real text. The Ephrem quote was chosen from a stretch free of the OCR's margin notes; other lines of the same stanza are broken by them. The Augustine Morals quote includes the NPNF editor's inline reference 'Matthew 8:32'. NOT RECORDED, for lack of a checkable public-domain or original text reached in this pass: Maximus the Confessor, Ambigua 10 (Scripture and creation as the two garments of the transfigured Christ, the natural and written law of equal honour; English only in Constas 2014, copyrighted); Evagrius's own teaching on 'natural contemplation' as a stage of prayer (modern translations only); Gerasimus and the lion (John Moschus, Spiritual Meadow 107, c. 600; no pre-1929 English; Moschus's own moral is that God showed how beasts obeyed Adam before the fall, not kindness as such); Basil's homily on thanksgiving (PG 31, 221) reading creatures 'as if they were letters and words'. Didymus the Blind (via Evagrius, in the same Socrates chapter) urged reflecting on providence 'in the difference of created forms, and the constitution of the universe'. NO EVIDENCE FOUND on either claim for: Ignatius, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Novatian, Ambrose, Pelagius, Paulinus of Nola, Amma Syncletica, Arsenius, Poemen, Moses the Black (his 'Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything' is about solitude, not nature), John Climacus (a Ladder quotation about animals on the Pan-Orthodox site is from a copyrighted modern translation and was not verified), Gregory of Nyssa in his own voice, and Gregory the Great in his own voice. Benedict of Nursia has only the crow he fed (Gregory, Dialogues 2.8), too thin for a position. Heterodox flags: Origen (condemned 553), Isaac (Church of the East), Tertullian (Montanist after c. 207; the Apology quote is from 197). Useful secondary survey with Father citations: G. Tanzella-Nitti, 'The Two Books Prior to the Scientific Revolution', Perspectives on Science and Christian Faith 57 (2005), but it misreads Augustine's Confessions 13.15 and Expositions 45.7 as nature texts.
